title: SYSK's Guatemalan Adventure, Part One
summary: Josh, Chuck and Jerry travel to Guatemala as guests of the Cooperative for Education (CoEd), a nonprofit that supplies textbooks and reading programs to rural indigenous schools. The episode covers the trip's background, Guatemala's civil war and the CIA-backed coup that ended the ten years of spring, travel precautions, Lake Atitlan and nearby towns, a Maximón ceremony, the 2005 Hurricane Stan mudslide aftermath in Panabaj, the 1990 Santiago Atitlán army massacre, and CoEd's self-sustaining textbook rental program and Culture of Reading program. Part two is promised for Thursday.

segments.title: Opening banter and Go To Meeting sponsor
segments.summary: The hosts open with a sponsor read for Go To Meeting, then a playful intro clip and introduce the two-part Guatemalan adventure episode with Jerry.

segments.title: How the Guatemala trip came about
segments.summary: Co-founder Dempsey (the transcript's 'Dempsey' is the nonprofit contact) emailed the hosts inviting them to see CoEd's work in Guatemala, sponsored with no strings attached. The hosts decided to bring Jerry and record a live on-the-road podcast asking whether education can alleviate poverty.

segments.title: Travel warnings and shots
segments.summary: The hosts describe reading the State Department travel warnings, which they found alarming, getting various inoculations, and Jerry and Chuck getting sick.

segments.title: Guatemala's civil war and the ten years of spring
segments.summary: The hosts summarize Guatemala's history: a dictatorship until the 1940s, a decade of liberal rule called the ten years of spring, the United Fruit Company's land redistribution dispute, the CIA-backed coup, and the civil war that followed, with a Truth Commission finding government soldiers committed most atrocities.

segments.title: Mayan population and Guatemalan economy
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the indigenous Mayan majority and languages, rural poverty rates, and the economy, with agriculture, remittances and tourism as the top three sectors.

segments.title: Education gap and the reading problem
segments.summary: A CoEd staffer's statistics are played: three of four rural first graders drop out before sixth grade, and many children do not learn to read until about third grade because teachers assume they cannot earlier. The hosts explain that CoEd's books are meant to change this.

segments.title: Flight to Guatemala and arrival
segments.summary: The hosts describe flying direct from Atlanta to Guatemala City, Josh sleeping under an airplane blanket, and the chaotic airport arrival where CoEd staff met them with a bus.

segments.title: Guatemala City and dinner with the founders
segments.summary: The hosts meet CoEd staff in Guatemala City, drink Gallo beer, struggle with an intro recording, and have dinner with co-founder Joe Burninger and staffer Holly, who explain the program. Jeff Burninger is described as co-founder with his brother Joe.

segments.title: Travel to Lake Atitlan and chicken buses
segments.summary: The hosts ride Mercedes sprinter vans to Santiago Atitlan, passing tobacco, coffee and banana farms. They explain that brightly painted chicken buses help people who cannot read pick the right bus, and describe Lake Atitlan's volcanic origin and cleanup.

segments.title: Pasada de Santiago lodging and town welcome
segments.summary: The group stays at Pasada de Santiago, a resort of stone cabanas. They describe the evergreen-straw and flower-petal carpet welcome used at the schools and a tour of the main square and a church where an American priest was murdered during the civil war.

segments.title: Visit to a student's family home
segments.summary: The hosts visit the home of Maria, a CoEd scholarship student, and her father, who is sending all three children to school despite the family's poverty. They describe the home and the family's gratitude.

segments.title: Maximon ceremony and truck ride
segments.summary: The hosts ride in small pickup trucks with A-frame beds to the outskirts of town. Chuck describes a visit to Maximon, a folk saint in a locked barn, with cigarettes and liquor offered and a funnel used to pour the drink into his mouth. Josh describes the Guaro sugarcane liquor and the ceremony's atmosphere.

segments.title: Panabaj mudslide aftermath
segments.summary: The hosts visit Panabaj, a village where Hurricane Stan mudslides in 2005 buried much of the community. They describe seventy-seven recovered bodies, about three hundred missing and presumed dead, and a boy who lost his parents and siblings and cares for other children.

segments.title: 1990 Santiago Atitlan army massacre
segments.summary: The hosts describe a 1990 massacre in Santiago Atitlán in which army soldiers fired on an unarmed crowd after soldiers from the garrison had abused residents. Fourteen people were killed and twenty-one wounded, memorials mark each spot, and the army later left the garrison.

segments.title: Lakeside evening and interview with Jeff Burninger
segments.summary: After a happy hour and dinner, the hosts interview co-founder Jeff Burninger, who describes how he went to Guatemala looking for volunteer work and discovered that the students had no books.

segments.title: CoEd textbook rental program
segments.summary: Jeff explains the self-sustaining textbook program: books are bought cheaply in bulk, students rent them for about two dollars a year, the fees fund a revolving escrow account to replace books, and research found parents could afford the fee and valued the books more. Five dollars buys one child a textbook for a year.

segments.title: Panabaj school donation and Culture of Reading
segments.summary: The hosts visit a poor highland school to donate textbooks and pencils, watch a corn dance, and meet principal Caroline Johnson, who describes why she moved to Guatemala and the Culture of Reading program. Part one closes with a teaser for part two and the textbook donation text-to-give pitch.
